grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakasvibira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakasvibira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pakati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pakati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: The Art of Hair Braiding ('Kuruka Musoro') in Zimbabwean Culture
cultural_notes.content: In Shona society, hair braiding ('kuruka musoro' or 'kuruka vhudzi') is both a treasured aesthetic art and an important social tradition. Across Harare, Bulawayo, and rural townships, women and girls gather at salons or on shaded verandas where skilled braiders weave intricate geometric patterns such as 'mabhanzi', three-strand plaits ('kuruka rutatu'), and neat cornrows ('lines'), often incorporating synthetic extensions ('rastasta').

cultural_notes.title: Miombo Woodlands ('Masango eMusasa') & Indigenous Flora of the Highveld
cultural_notes.content: Much of central Zimbabwe lies within the southern African Miombo woodland belt, dominated by indigenous 'musasa' (Brachystegia spiciformis) and 'mnondo' trees. In spring ('chirimo', September–October), new leaves ('mashizha') emerge in brilliant shades of copper, crimson, and lime green before turning deep green during the summer rains.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pamusoro')

Look at how location is expressed with 'pamusoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('parutivi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'parutivi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('imwe')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'imwe' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

cultural_notes.title: Miombo Woodlands ('Masango eMusasa') & Indigenous Flora of the Highveld

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nezvipfuyo'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nezvipfuyo'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'zvipfuyo' forms 'nezvipfuyo'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

cultural_notes.title: Thatching Grass ('Huswa Hwekupfurira Dzimba') & Dry-Season Grazing

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: The Art of Hair Braiding ('Kuruka Musoro') in Zimbabwean Culture
cultural_notes.content: In Shona society, hair braiding ('kuruka musoro' or 'kuruka vhudzi') is both a treasured aesthetic art and an important social tradition. Across Harare, Bulawayo, and rural townships, women and girls gather at salons or on shaded verandas where skilled braiders weave intricate geometric patterns such as 'mabhanzi', three-strand plaits ('kuruka rutatu'), and neat cornrows ('lines'), often incorporating synthetic extensions ('rastasta').

Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ineruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ineruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('vaviri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'vaviri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('Imwe')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'Imwe' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('egirini')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'egirini'. grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('Shangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'Shangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

shona_text: Vanhu vazhinji, varume nevakadzi varikuratidza kuti varikufamba vachipinda nepasi pemudhuri, mumwe mukadzi arikumberi akapfeka shangu chena nemudhebhe wesatani watingati ndewe jini akabata mbozhanhare neruoko rwake rwerudyi, arikuratidza kuti arikutotaura nemunhu pambozhanhare yacho, sezvo akaiisa panzeve yokuruoko rwerudyi. Pane varume vana murume nemudzimai mumwechete murume mumwe akapfeka chipika chichena akatarisa kumberi kunoiita kunge munhu ari kutaura. Mudzimai akabata chirebvu chake achitaridza kusuruvara.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akapfeka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akapfeka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

title: Chidzidzo 1: Maruva ari kutengeswa akawanda pamusika wawo....
shona_text: Maruva ari kutengeswa akawanda pamusika wawo. Mamwe ari mumagaba mamwa akasungwa. Pane mashedhi akavakwa mune vanhu mukati vanotengesa. Mamwe akagadzikwa papevhimendi. Pane murume ane jinhi rebhuruu nekepesi tema akarembedza masiki ari kupfuura akamatarira kuruboshwe rwake. Pane umwe murume akamafuratira nevamwe vari kufamba. Serotepi dzakagadzikwa patafura chena. Imwe itema, imwe chena imwe tsvuku. Dzine mizera yakasiyana imwe ikuru imwe idiki.
english_translation: At a flower market, potted plants and tied bouquets are displayed under market sheds and along the pavement as passersby in jeans and caps look on. Nearby on a white table sit rolls of black, white, and red adhesive tape in various sizes.

title: Chidzidzo 1: Nzvimbo ine sora rakaoma rinoratidza kuti...
shona_text: Nzvimbo ine sora rakaoma rinoratidza kuti rava nenguva risina kunaiwa nemvura zvabva zvaita kuti tifungidzire kuti iyi inguva yechando kana nguva yechirimo. Nechekumberi kwacho kuri kubuda hunde dzemiti inoratidza kuti miti mukuru kwazvo. Mutambi wenhabvu akamira munhandare iri padhuze nedzimba. Mutambi akapfeka nguo dzokutambisa bhora pamwe chete nebhutsu dzekutamba nadzo bhora. Akapfeka hembe dzerudzi rwebhuruu nemitsara michena. Kumashure kwakamirawo mumwe akapfeka hembe tsvuku.
english_translation: Dry grass shows that it has gone a long time without rain during the cool dry winter (chando) or hot dry spring (chirimo), with large tree trunks rising ahead. On a neighbourhood pitch near houses, football players in blue-and-white and red kits stand in football boots.

dialogue.english: Dry grass indicates a long spell without rain during the winter (chando) or spring (chirimo) dry season, with large tree trunks visible ahead.

title: Chidzidzo 59: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso...
shona_text: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso hwake hausi kuonekwa asi pane ruoko rwuri mumusoro runoita senge ndiro ruri kugadzira bvudzi. Ari kumonwa tumabhanzi turi kuinda tuchidonhera kusvika nechekuda kuenzana namapendekete. Bvudzi idema pasi asi pamusoro rakatsvukuruka. Rakapfava zvinoratidza kuti rakaiswa mushonga. Vanhu vaviri vomutambo wonhabvu. Vakapfeka mayunifomu akafanana. Umwe chete akaisa chichena pamusoro. Vanoratidza kuti varipakudzidzira mutambo wawo uye vose vari kukwikwidzana kuti vagone kukava bhora riri nechepasi.
english_translation: A woman is having her hair styled. Her face is not visible, but a stylist's hand can be seen braiding her hair into neat twists that fall toward her shoulders. The hair is black at the roots and reddish-brown toward the tips, looking soft and treated. In another scene, two football players in matching uniforms—one wearing a white cap—are training and competing to kick the ball on the ground.

dialogue.shona: Munhukadzi ari kugadzirwa musoro wake. Uso hwake hausi kuonekwa asi pane ruoko rwuri mumusoro runoita senge ndiro ruri kugadzira bvudzi.
dialogue.english: A woman is having her hair styled; her face is not visible, but a hand can be seen working on her hair.

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('yeruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'yeruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akagadzikwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akagadzikwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('paneruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'paneruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

title: Chidzidzo 62: Munhurume wechiAfrica akamira akabata machira ane...
shona_text: Munhurume wechiAfrica akamira akabata machira ane ruvara rutatu achiratidza kudhekoreta panzvimbo yaakamira. Mbatatisi nhatu dziri pabhodhi rineruvara ruchena idzo dzine ruvara rwakaita goridhe dzirikuratidza hutano. Imwe ihombe dzimwe idiki. Mundiro yemuti iyi muzere madora . Madora aya akakangwa zvakanaka akasanganiswa nematamati nehanyanisi. Ivhu rakawanda rakaunganidzwa rakatsetseka zvinobva zvaita kuti tifungidzire kuti panzvimbo iyi inzvimbo ine zvicherwa zvinocherwa. Ivhu iri ndiro rinocherwa kubva pasi panenge pachicherwa zvicherwa izvi.
english_translation: An African man stands holding three-coloured cloths to decorate the place where he stands. Three golden, healthy-looking potatoes rest on a white board—one large and the others smaller. A wooden bowl is filled with mopane caterpillars (madora), well-roasted and mixed with tomatoes and onions. Nearby, heaps of excavated soil indicate a mining area where minerals are dug from underground.

title: Chidzidzo 64: Mushina unoshandiswa kunamirira mitengo kumadziro uye...
shona_text: Mushina unoshandiswa kunamirira mitengo kumadziro uye pazvinhu zviri kutengeswa. Marobhotsi anowanikwa mumaguta. Anoita kuti mota dzisabonderane. Bhutsu yegumbo rwokurudyi ine mavara akasiyana siyana anosanganisira ruvara rwendarama, rwebhuruu, rweorenji, rwuchena uyewo ruvara rutema.

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive

title: Chidzidzo 1: Nzvimbo inoratidza kuti panogadzirwa dzimotokari. Pane...

Panzvimbo inoiswa vhiri paneo munhurume mumwechete akarara pakadhibokisi achigadzira motokari iyi. Miti dzakawanda dzine mizera yakasiyana. Mumwe une mashizha akawanda akasvibira egirini. title: Chidzidzo 1: Mukereke vanhu vakagara pasi, kune mumwe...

Pane vakagara pasi kune vanhu vakapfeka hembe ine ruvara rutsvuku koitawo vamwe vakapfeka hembe dzine ruvara ruchena Zvituro zvakatsvetwa zvakarundana zvakarongana zvichiratidza kuti zvituro izvi zvakagadzirwa nematanda uye zvituro zvokuzororera. title: Chidzidzo 1: Nzvimbo yakashongedza zvinoratidza kuti pane zvakakosha...
shona_text: Nzvimbo yakashongedza zvinoratidza kuti pane zvakakosha mutambo wakakosha unoda kuitwapo, pane mabharuma akatenderedza ane ruvara rwebhuruu , nepingi neruvara ruchena , pane matafura nezvigaro zvakaiswa machira machena neruvara rwebhuruu uye pane keke rinoratidza kuti rine ruvara rwebhuruu namawaini aripo zvose izvi zvinoenderana namakara aripamabharuma kana kuti ruvara rwemabharuma. Gaka regirini rine tumunzwa rine kuzasi kweyero rakabatwa mumaoko pane mugaka uripo uri mumunda une mashizha egirini ane kayero nemaruva eyero. Vanhu vazhinji varikufamba pamusika. title: Chidzidzo 1: Nzvimbo inoratidza kuti inesora rakaoma, risina...
shona_text: Nzvimbo inoratidza kuti inesora rakaoma, risina utano zvinobva zvaita kuti tifungidzire kuti pava nenguva pakareba pasina kumbonaiwa nemvura uye tibve taona kuti iyi inguva yechando kana kuti nguva yechirimo sezvo nguva iyi isinganyanyi kunaya mvura. Mujinga regomo guru mune mhuka dzirikufura huswa. Mhuka idzi dzinosanganisira Mvuu uye Nzou imwe chete. Mudzimai kana kuti musikana akatarisa pasi. Akarukwa musoro wake achiiswa mitsetse uye twunyeredzi. Akafukidzawo mhino nomuromo wake nemasiki. Vaimbi vari kuimba nziyo dzejerusarema. Vakapfeka nhumbi dzechinyakare izvo zvinoita kuti vanhu vange vachifara vange vachinzwa kusununguka munguva iyoyo.
english_translation: Dry savanna grass shows that it is the dry winter or spring season (chando/chirimo) when little rain falls, while at the foot of a large hill hippos (mvuu) and an elephant (nzou) graze. Nearby, a young woman with star-patterned braids wears a face mask, and traditional performers in ancestral attire sing and dance Jerusarema (Mbende) songs with joy.

Mujinga regomo guru mune mhuka dzirikufura huswa. Mhuka idzi dzinosanganisira Mvuu uye Nzou imwe chete.

title: Chidzidzo 61: Vanhu vakaungana mubani vese vane migomo...
shona_text: Vanhu vakaungana mubani vese vane migomo zvinove zvigubu zvekuratidza kuti varikucherera mvura parutivi pavo pane Jojo tengi rakavakirwa pamusoro rikatsveta pamusoro pechi mudhuri zvichiratidza kuti ndimo murikubva mvura yavari kuchereredza. Nzvimbo inemiti yakasiyana siyana inosanganisira muti wemumango. Muti wemumango una mashizha aneruvara rwegirinhi. Koita zvakare maruva aripedyo neruzhowa. Maruva aya anamashizha aneruvara rwegirinhi neruvara rwepingi. Mudzimai mutsvuku akashongedza kumeso kwake akanyora tsiye dzake zvakanaka akapenda kumeso kwake nokupenda miromo yake akapfeka mhete munzeve make dzeruvara ruchena akapfeka hembe isina maoko neruvara ruchena neruvara rutema akagadzira musoro wake zvakanaka akaisa shedhi akapushira bvudzi rake kumashure akasunga chipomupomu cherudzi rusiri rwebvudzi rake.

Nearby grows a variety of trees including a mango tree with green leaves, alongside flowers with green leaves and pink blossoms near a fence. A light-complexioned woman has neatly styled her eyebrows, applied makeup, put on white earrings and a sleeveless black-and-white top, and tied her hair back.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakaungana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakaungana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('zvinove')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvinove' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Community Water Points, 'Jojo' Storage Tanks & Backyard Mango Trees

title: Chidzidzo 65: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori...
shona_text: Rori huru kwazvo rakamira zvaro. Rori iri rine musoro muchena uye rakanaka zvikuru pakutarisa. Rinoratidza kuti rinogona kutakura zvinhu zvakawanda kwazvo uye rori iri riri panzvimbo inoratidza kuti inzvimbo yekuwedzera mafuta. Shangu dzekurudyi nedzekuruboshwe. Dzine ruvara rwebhuruu neruchena. Dzinoratidza kuti dzakambopfekwa nekuti dzaakukwatanuka. Dzine tambo chena. Shangu idzi dzinogona kupfekwa zvose nevanhurume kana vanhukadzi. Vanhu vakamira padivi pemotokari dzemarudzi rwemakombi mukati meguta nechekumberi kune imba hombe yemudurikanidzwa yakabaka magetsi mukati mayo. Masvingo eGreat Zimbabwe izvi zvinova zvivakwa zvematombo zviri munzvimbo yeMasvingo. Inzvimbo inonyanyawo kushanyirwa nevanhu vachiona mararamiro aiitawo vanhu kare uyewo pane vanhu vari kuratidza kuti vakamira vauya kuzoshanya panzvimbo iyi.
english_translation: A huge truck is parked; it has a handsome white cab, can carry heavy loads, and is stopped at a fuel station. Nearby are left and right blue-and-white shoes with white laces that can be worn by men or women. In the city, people stand beside commuter minibuses (makombi) with a lit multi-storey building ahead. Finally, the stone walls of Great Zimbabwe in Masvingo are shown—a famous heritage site visited by many people to see how ancestors lived long ago.

title: Chidzidzo 99: Muti mukuru kwazvo une mashizha akasvibira....
shona_text: Muti mukuru kwazvo une mashizha akasvibira. Muti uyu unoratidza kuti uri kuwana mvura yakakwana nokuti mashizha awo akakura uye akawanda. Pasi pemuti uyu pane ivhu rakatsvuka huye pane twumasora twushoma. Shangu tema dzakavharika kumberi nekumasure. Dzine rudzi rwejombo uye dzine twusimbi twuri kuonekera nechekure twunopenya penya padivi padzo. Dzine tambo dzokusungisa. Nzvimbo iri pakati peguta. Pane vanhu vari kufamba vachienda kumativi akasiyana. Panewo robhoti rinobatsira kuti mota dzifambe zvakanaka. Nechekumberi kune zvivako zviri kubudira, zvivako izvi zvakavakwa zvichikwira mudenga. Nzvimbo iri pedyo nemugwagwa une tara.Ine huswa husina kunyanya kukura.Huswa hwacho hwakaita kutsvukuruka.Panewo miti ine maruva.Maruva acho matsvuku uye mamwe akada kuita pingi.Mashizha emiti iyi ndeegirini.
english_translation: A very large tree has lush green leaves, showing that it receives plenty of water because its leaves are big and abundant, with red soil and a little grass beneath it. Nearby are closed black boots with shiny metal eyelets and laces. In the city centre, people walk in different directions while traffic lights help cars flow smoothly and high-rise buildings rise ahead. Along a tarred road with short brownish grass stand flowering trees with red and pink blossoms and green leaves.

title: Chidzidzo 1: Mudzimai werudzi rwechichena akamira. Akapfeka nguwo...
shona_text: Mudzimai werudzi rwechichena akamira. Akapfeka nguwo yekumusoro ine ruvara rwepingi neruchena. Kuzasi akapfeka jinhi rebhuru. Kutsoka dzake akapfeka shangu dzine ruvara ruchena uyezve akapfeka masokisi ane ruvara rwepingi. Mudzimai uyu akabereka bhegi rine ruvara rweyero, bhuru nepingi. Mugwagwa miviri inemhararano. Mumwe mugwagwa urikufamba motokari. Mugwagwa urikufamba motokari uyu wakavharwa nemasimbi mapfupi ane ruvara rwuchena nerwutema Pane murume akazembera imwe simbi. Chitoro chinotengesa zvinhu zvokushongedza muviri zviri kuwonekwa pane pazvidhori zvichena muzasi zvakapfekedzwa manekiresi. Nechekumusoro kune amwe manekiresi ari kurembera zvimwe zviri kumudhuri zvakasangana nemhete. Motikari mbiri dzine rudzi ruchena dziri kufamba mumugwagwa. Mujinga memugwagwa mune maruva akadonhera pasi epepuru. Madzibaba vakapfeka vanenguwo tsvuku muhuro nemudonzvo mutsvuku. Vakapfeka hembe dzeruvara ruchena nerepepoo. Vakamira panechimba chinoratidza kuti chakavakwa nemapango. Panemunhu wavarikutaura naye anoratidza kuti munhu wechitendero chavo vane zvavari kutsimbidzira kwaari. Vakapfeka nhumbi dzechitendero uye zvinechekuita nekunamata.

Inside a jewellery shop, necklaces and earrings are displayed on white busts, while Apostolic church elders (Madzibaba) in white garments, red stoles, and staffs converse earnestly by a timber shelter.

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akamira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akamira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('chinotengesa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'chinotengesa' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pakati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pakati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'pachigaro' = on the chair, 'patafura' = on the table, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'mundiro' = in the plate, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (pachigaro) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nepakati'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nepakati'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'pakati' forms 'nepakati'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakawanda')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakawanda' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('inoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'inoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('ina')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'ina' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'Chineruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('chakaiswa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'chakaiswa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('chinoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'chinoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mutema')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mutema'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), grey ('gireyi'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'anoratidza' = shows), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').

grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nepakati'. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anorembera')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anorembera' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: The Art of Hair Braiding ('Kuruka Musoro') in Zimbabwean Culture
cultural_notes.content: In Shona society, hair braiding ('kuruka musoro' or 'kuruka vhudzi') is both a treasured aesthetic art and an important social tradition. Across Harare, Bulawayo, and rural townships, women and girls gather at salons or on shaded verandas where skilled braiders weave intricate geometric patterns such as 'mabhanzi', three-strand plaits ('kuruka rutatu'), and neat cornrows ('lines'), often incorporating synthetic extensions ('rastasta').

points: Miombo Woodlands ('Masango eMusasa') & Indigenous Flora of the Highveld: Much of central Zimbabwe lies within the southern African Miombo woodland belt, dominated by indigenous 'musasa' (Brachystegia spiciformis) and 'mnondo' trees.

Visual Art, Portraiture ('Mifananidzo') & Contemporary Youth Expression in Zimbabwe: In contemporary urban Zimbabwe, visual art ('mifananidzo') spans gallery painting at the National Gallery of Zimbabwe in Harare and Bulawayo, street murals, photography, and modern body art.

Slow-Cooked Beef Tripe ('Maguru eMombe') & Traditional Shona Delicacies: In Zimbabwean cuisine, beef tripe and offal ('maguru nematumbu emombe') slow-simmered until tender ('akabikwa zvine unyanzvi akaibva zvakanaka') is a beloved traditional dish.

Backyard Peach Trees ('Mupichisi'), Brick Stacking & Haulage 'Magonyeti': This vivid passage captures three everyday sights in Zimbabwean peri-urban neighbourhoods: a fruiting peach tree ('muti wemupichisi') in the yard, stacks of clay bricks ('zvidhinha') ready for home extensions, and a massive intercity haulage truck—universally called a 'gonyeti'—parked along the main road..

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('rakasvipira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rakasvipira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('rinoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'rinoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Miombo Woodlands ('Masango eMusasa') & Indigenous Flora of the Highveld
cultural_notes.content: Much of central Zimbabwe lies within the southern African Miombo woodland belt, dominated by indigenous 'musasa' (Brachystegia spiciformis) and 'mnondo' trees. In spring ('chirimo', September–October), new leaves ('mashizha') emerge in brilliant shades of copper, crimson, and lime green before turning deep green during the summer rains.

active_exercises.prompt: In a Zimbabwean city, if a driver says 'Mota dzakamira parobhoti dzichimirira mwenje wegirinhi', where are the cars stopped?
options: At a rural bus stop waiting for passengers
At the traffic light waiting for the green light
Inside a garage having their tyres repaired
Beside a river bridge that is under construction
active_exercises.correct_answer: At the traffic light waiting for the green light
active_exercises.explanation: 'Robhoti' (plural 'marobhotsi') is the standard Shona word for a traffic light, and 'mwenje wegirinhi' is the green light.

active_exercises.prompt: How would you say 'Open the door quickly!' in Shona using the vocabulary pattern from this unit?
active_exercises.correct_answer: Vhura musuwo nekukasira!
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vhura' means 'open!', 'musuwo' is 'door', and 'nekukasira' (or 'nekukurumidza') means 'quickly'.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new morning exchange into English: 'Mangwanani baba, mamuka sei?'
options: Good evening Mother, how was your day?
Hello my friend, where are you going today?
Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.correct_answer: Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mangwanani' = 'Good morning', 'baba' = 'Father', and 'mamuka sei?' = 'how did you wake up?'.
